question_html: Which of the following correctly distinguishes an 'audit' from an 'investigation'?

options.A: An audit and an investigation are identical in scope and purpose
options.B: An investigation has a narrow, specific purpose (e.g. probing suspected fraud), while an audit has a general and broad scope aimed at expressing an opinion on financial statements as a whole
options.C: An investigation is always voluntary, while an audit is always mandatory

answer_html:

An audit is not an official investigation into alleged wrongdoing; the auditor lacks the specific legal powers of search or recording sworn statements that an investigation may require. The scope of audit is general and broad, while the scope of investigation is specific and narrow.

question_html: Which of the following is an example of a 'practical' limitation (as opposed to a 'legal' limitation) on the auditor's ability to obtain audit evidence, under the 'nature of audit procedures' factor?

options.A: The auditor testing only a sample of transactions and balances rather than every single one, since it is not possible to test all of them

The study material distinguishes practical limitations (e.g. testing samples rather than all transactions) from legal limitations (e.g. management not being legally compellable to provide complete information) on the auditor's ability to obtain evidence.

question_html: Why does the 'timeliness of financial reporting' represent an inherent limitation of audit?

options.A: Because financial statements are never prepared on time

question_html: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes a 'review' from an 'audit'?

options.A: A review provides a higher level of assurance than an audit

question_html: An assurance engagement relating to the examination of prospective financial information (such as a forecast) provides:

options.A: A reasonable level of assurance, identical to an audit
options.B: A limited level of assurance, identical to a review
options.C: An absolute level of assurance, since projections are inherently more reliable than historical data
options.D: A 'moderate' level of assurance, since the practitioner can only report that nothing has come to their attention to suggest the underlying assumptions are unreasonable

answer_html:
D. A 'moderate' level of assurance, since the practitioner can only report that nothing has come to their attention to suggest the underlying assumptions are unreasonable

Since prospective financial information is future-oriented, the auditor cannot express an opinion on whether the projected results will actually be achieved. The practitioner instead reports that nothing has come to their attention suggesting the assumptions are unreasonable - providing only a 'moderate' level of assurance.

subject: Auditing and Ethics
case_facts_html: Kavya, Rehan and Nitin are CA Intermediate students who recently attended a guest lecture on auditing. During a discussion afterwards, Nitin remarked that once a company's financial statements are audited, the audit report acts as a 100% guarantee that the company's affairs are completely free of any error or fraud. Kavya disagreed, pointing out that an audit is based on testing selected samples of transactions rather than every single transaction recorded in the books. Rehan added that even if the auditor exercises due professional skill, they may still be misled if an employee deliberately fabricates supporting documents to conceal a fraud.
question_html: Is Nitin's understanding of the assurance provided by an audit report correct?

options.A: Yes, an audit report is a 100% guarantee that the financial statements are completely free of error or fraud
options.B: Yes, but only for listed companies, since they are subject to stricter regulation
options.C: No; an audit provides no assurance at all, and financial statements are just as reliable whether audited or not
options.D: No; an audit provides only reasonable assurance, which is a high level of assurance, but not an absolute guarantee, since the auditor cannot reduce audit risk to zero

answer_html:
D. No; an audit provides only reasonable assurance, which is a high level of assurance, but not an absolute guarantee, since the auditor cannot reduce audit risk to zero

As per SA 200, the auditor is not expected to, and cannot, reduce audit risk to zero, and therefore cannot obtain absolute assurance that financial statements are free from material misstatement. Nitin's belief in a '100% guarantee' is incorrect.
